claims.text: Controlled additions of light elements such as Al or Mg can induce moderate lattice distortion in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Moderate lattice distortion is key to concurrently enhancing mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance while maintaining low density.
The size differences of the added light elements create controlled lattice distortions.
Controlled lattice distortions impede dislocation passage.
Impeded dislocation passage enhances mechanical strength.
Light-element-induced lattice distortion stabilizes grain boundaries.
Light-element-induced lattice distortion modifies atomic-scale diffusion pathways.
Grain-boundary stabilization slows diffusion-controlled degradation.
Slower diffusion-controlled degradation improves corrosion resistance.
Slower diffusion-controlled degradation improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The proposed light-element additions cause only a minimal increase in density.
The modified alloy will have greater tensile strength than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have greater hardness than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have a lower corrosion rate than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will show less oxidation mass gain than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will retain low density relative to the baseline.
Excessive light-element concentration can produce excessive lattice distortion and phase separation.
Excessive light-element concentration can cause embrittlement.
The mechanism may cease to apply under extreme temperatures or in non-oxidizing environments where diffusion is not the primary degradation mode.
A controlled comparison will test modified and baseline alloys under identical tensile, hardness, electrochemical-corrosion, oxidation, and density measurements.
